long_biography.plain_text:
As a child in The Three Keatons, Joseph Frank Keaton learned to absorb acrobatic falls without changing his expression. The travelling vaudeville act gave him timing, physical control and an instinct for finding comedy in real objects. When he encountered Roscoe Arbuckle and a motion-picture camera in 1917, the veteran stage performer quickly recognised film as a different medium rather than a photographed version of theatre.

Independent production gave ‘Buster’ Keaton room to unite acting, direction, writing, stunt design and camera effects. Sherlock Jr., The General and other features turned machines, buildings and moving landscapes into parts of the performance. A move to MGM ended much of that autonomy, but he continued working in films, gag writing, television and commercials. Renewed appreciation brought restorations and retrospectives, while an Honorary Academy Award in 1960 recognised the distinctive comedies whose technical clarity and impassive hero still influence filmmakers.

Keaton was the creative principal of a dedicated production company and independent film platform, but producer Joseph Schenck supplied important corporate, financing and distribution infrastructure. Founder is used for Keaton's core creative enterprise, not to imply sole ownership of every associated company or film right.
The Kansas Historical Society identifies Piqua in Woodson County, Kansas. Modern references sometimes describe the place as Piqua or nearby Pickway; the official state-history wording is used.

No strong evidence established a secondary nationality. Keaton died before modern social platforms, so no personal LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, X, YouTube, TikTok or personal website can be verified; only the dedicated Wikipedia article is proposed.
